source.title: Xetrieval: Explaining Dense Retrieval through Feature Elicitation
source.authors: Zhi-Xi Cai; Jun Bai; Yang Liu; Jia-Qi Li; Yi-Chi Zhang; Tai-Chuan Li; Zhuo-Fan Chen; Zi-Xia Jia; Zi-Long Zheng; Wen-Ge Rong

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or cut-off; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE-derived features in dense retrieval embeddings are interpretable and affect retrieval scores, extending feature-dictionary evidence to dense retrievers rather than testing toy-model superposition or LLM internal representations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on feature description–activation agreement and feature-span interventions on retrieval scores. Retrieval benchmark gains from feature elicitation, latency results, and most task-level steering results are not rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions. Cited findings from other papers are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAEs on frozen dense-retriever embeddings (e5-large) as an explanation tool. Every reported result compares its own method, Xetrieval (feature elicitors plus a shared SAE), against an SAE baseline: detection scores, intervention score deltas, task-level steering and retrieval gains. It never asks whether superposition holds or whether SAEs recover the model's features as such. Superposition is cited only as motivation. The Untrained SAE appears only as a control in the description evaluation. The text does not state how SAE compares with Untrained SAE, only that Xetrieval scores higher than both. No result therefore bears on V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Xetrieval yields more interpretable features than an SAE baseline, finds feature spans with stronger influence on the retriever's original scores, and gives more effective task-level steering. They also say semantic presentation shapes which interpretable features are available.
record.recipe_differences: Uses feature elicitors, auxiliary document views, and a shared TopK SAE on dense retrieval embeddings; it does not reproduce the toy-network setup or measurements of Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature descriptions and the learned SAE dictionary depend on the chosen LLMs, prompts, training corpora, and feature-elicitation views; the paper notes these dependencies but does not systematically vary them in the reported feature-intervention results.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting document embeddings onto spans of SAE decoder directions shared by query and document changes query–document cosine similarity. Erasing the span lowers it and retaining it raises it, on seven datasets (Fig. 6). Non-overlapping features show the opposite response.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In dense retriever embeddings, SAE decoder directions active in both query and document causally carry relevance-score information.

record.problems: Feature-interpretation and detection evaluation rely on LLM outputs. The feature-intervention outcomes are presented graphically without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The evidence concerns dense retrieval embeddings, not LLM internal activations or toy-model superposition.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant rows omitted. Retrieval-performance comparisons, task-level modulation, and latency results were left out because they measure retrieval utility or efficiency rather than the versions’ named feature-recovery or superposition claims.

untested.parts: Toy networks, sparsity vs dimensionality, nearly orthogonal directions, phase transition, geometry: none studied.
Capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features: not studied.
Polysemantic neurons and their alternative causes: not studied.

No test of features being spread across neurons. SAE recovery is assumed and used as a tool in retriever embeddings, not tested against a null. The text does not report SAE vs Untrained SAE separately.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not measured. The paper only notes that dictionaries depend on the training corpus.
The paper uses spans of 1-D decoder directions but does not test one-dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: This is an explainable-retrieval method paper, so the reader's T3/tests guess is wrong. The Untrained SAE control could in principle bear on V4 (SAE features beat random ones). However, Fig. 5 is described only as Xetrieval outscoring both SAE and Untrained SAE; no SAE-vs-untrained statement or number is given. All key evidence is figure-only, with no uncertainty reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks, feature sparsity versus dimensionality, overlapping nearly orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests SAE-derived features in dense retrieval embeddings, not feature distribution across neurons or SAE recovery in LLM internal activations.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units; it notes corpus dependence but does not measure stability across corpora or methods.
Uses decoder directions and spans of directions, but does not test whether the underlying features are necessarily one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Feature-description evaluation and pair-level interventions on the tested dense retrieval embeddings
reader_labels.reason: Xetrieval descriptions align more closely with activation patterns than SAE and Untrained SAE, and its selected feature spans change original retrieval scores more strongly than matched-count SAE spans (r1–r3). This is evidence for useful SAE-derived features in this setting, not evidence about LLM internal activations.
